name.text: WAT 17.1: No New Is Good News!

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write an instrument class with an initialiser and two methods, plus two functions that build one and read its counter.

How this works in Python

You have written Java classes for years, so read what follows for the differences rather than for the concept. Here is a class that remembers a running total, first in Java.

public class Tally {
    private int count;

    public Tally(int start) {
        this.count = start;
    }

    public void add(int amount) {
        this.count += amount;
    }
}

Here is the same class in Python.

class Tally:
    def __init__(self, start: int) -> None:
        self.count = start

    def add(self, amount: int) -> None:
        self.count += amount

Five things changed. Take them one at a time.

The class header carries no modifier

No public, no final, no abstract. The word class, the name, a colon, and an indented body. That is the whole header.

The initialiser is not named after the class

Java makes you repeat Tally, so renaming the class means renaming its constructor too. Python calls the method __init__ in every class ever written, so there is nothing to keep in step. Two underscores at each end of a name make a dunder, short for double underscore, and this one is said out loud as "dunder init".

It is not quite a constructor either. Python builds the empty object first, then hands it to __init__ to fill in. __init__ hands nothing back, which is why it is annotated -> None like any other method that returns nothing. Return a value from it and Python raises TypeError.

There is no new

Call the class itself, the way you would call a function.

running = Tally(0)
running.add(5)

self is written out every time

Java hides this and lets you drop it, so a bare count inside a method might be a field, a parameter or a local, and you read the rest of the class to find out which. Python makes the receiver the first parameter of every method and makes you type it. self.count is unmistakably the attribute, and count is unmistakably local.

You never pass it at the call site. Writing running.add(5) passes running in as self and 5 in as amount. The name self is a convention rather than a keyword, and every Python programmer keeps to it. Leave it off a method header and Python raises TypeError the first time anyone calls that method.

Because self is an ordinary parameter, a method is an ordinary function that happens to live inside a class. Tally.add(running, 5) does exactly what running.add(5) does, and one of the tests below proves it on your own class.

There are no field declarations

Java lists count at the top of the class and the compiler rejects any name it has not seen there. Python has no such list. Python calls a field an attribute, and an attribute starts existing the moment you assign to it. Assign every one of them to self inside __init__, so a reader meets the full set in one place and no instance ever goes without one.

Assigning a name in the class body instead, outside every method, means something else entirely. The next tier of this topic is about what it means, and about the bug it causes. Until then, put every attribute in __init__.

There is no private

One more absence. No protected, no package scope, nothing. Every attribute is reachable from outside, from anywhere, always. A single leading underscore on a name asks other programmers to keep out.

self._recalibrations = 0

It is a request, not a lock. Nothing enforces it, and one of the functions below makes you read such an attribute from outside the class to prove it. Python does have a second trick, written with two leading underscores, and the last tier of this topic covers what it really does.

Your task

Write one class and two functions.

  • Instrument, built from a tag and a reading. __init__ stores both and starts self._recalibrations at 0.
  • describe() returns f"{tag} reads {reading}", for example TI-101 reads 21.5.
  • recalibrate(reading) replaces the stored reading and adds one to self._recalibrations.
  • first_reading(tag, reading) builds one Instrument and returns its describe().
  • peek_underscore(instrument) reads _recalibrations off the instrument from outside the class and returns f"the underscore stopped nothing: {..}" with the count in the slot.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Do not write the word new. Calling the class is the whole of it.
  • Name the initialiser __init__. A method named Instrument is a Java constructor that will never run.
  • Write self as the first parameter of every method, and never pass it at a call site.
  • Assign every attribute to self inside __init__. Declare nothing in the class body.
  • Do not write a method whose name starts with get_ or set_. Reach for the attribute directly.
  • Annotate every signature. __init__ hands nothing back, so it gets -> None. Never annotate self.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

testcode.text: gauge = Instrument("TI-101", 21.5) print(gauge.describe()) gauge.recalibrate(22.0) print(gauge.describe()) print(first_reading("PI-204", 3.0))

expected.text: TI-101 reads 21.5 TI-101 reads 22.0 PI-204 reads 3.0

testcode.text: one = Instrument("FT-9", 1.0) two = Instrument("FT-9", 1.0) one.recalibrate(9.5) print(one.describe(), "|", two.describe()) print(peek_underscore(one), "|", peek_underscore(two)) print(Instrument.describe(one))

expected.text: FT-9 reads 9.5 | FT-9 reads 1.0 the underscore stopped nothing: 1 | the underscore stopped nothing: 0 FT-9 reads 9.5

testcode.text: import inspect src = inspect.getsource(Instrument) assert "def __init__" in src, "rule broken: fill the instance in __init__" assert "self:" not in src, "rule broken: never annotate self" assert "-> None" in src, "rule broken: __init__ hands nothing back, so annotate it -> None" assert "get_" not in src and "set_" not in src, "rule broken: no accessor pair" assert "Instrument(" in inspect.getsource(first_reading), "rule broken: build it by calling the class" declared = set(Instrument.__dict__) | set(getattr(Instrument, "__annotations__", {})) assert "tag" not in declared and "reading" not in declared, "rule broken: attributes are born in __init__" fresh = Instrument("ZZ-9", 0.0) print(hasattr(fresh, "tag"), hasattr(fresh, "_recalibrations")) fresh.recalibrate(1.5) fresh.recalibrate(2.5) print(peek_underscore(fresh)) print(Instrument.describe(fresh))

expected.text: True True the underscore stopped nothing: 2 ZZ-9 reads 2.5

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write a station class whose readings belong to each instance, plus a function that shows what goes wrong when they do not.

How this works in Python

Here is a small class in Java.

public class Station {
    private final String name;
    private final List<Integer> readings = new ArrayList<>();

    public Station(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    public void addReading(int value) {
        this.readings.add(value);
    }
}

Here is the same class in Python.

class Station:
    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None:
        self.name = name
        self.readings: list[int] = []

    def add_reading(self, value: int) -> None:
        self.readings.append(value)

Four things changed. Take them one at a time.

There are no field declarations

Java lists name and readings at the top of the class. Python has no such list. Python calls a field an attribute, and an attribute starts existing the moment you assign to it. The place where you assign it decides who owns it.

__init__ is the initialiser, not the constructor

Two underscores at each end of a name make a dunder, short for double underscore. You met the word in the previous tier of this topic. Say this one out loud as "dunder init". Python builds the empty object first, then calls __init__ to fill it in. You never write new. Call the class itself.

north = Station("north")

self is written out every time

Java hides this and lets you drop it. Python makes it the first parameter of every method and makes you type it. You never pass it at the call site. Writing north.add_reading(10) passes north in as self. Leave self off a method and Python raises TypeError the first time anyone calls that method.

There are no access modifiers

No private, no public, no final. Every attribute is reachable from outside. A leading underscore on a name asks other programmers to keep out. It is a promise, not a lock. Because everything is reachable anyway, a getX and setX pair buys nothing, so Python code reads and writes the attribute directly.

Now the trap. It catches Java developers more often than anything else in this topic. Assign a name in the class body, outside every method, and you have not declared a field. You have written the equivalent of a Java static field.

class LeakyStation:
    readings: list[int] = []
    count: int = 0

There is one list and every instance shares it. Append through one station and every other station sees the new reading. The integer fails the other way round. self.count += 1 reads the shared 0, adds one, then binds the result to the instance. The class attribute never changes, so one station grows a count of its own while LeakyStation.count still reports 0.

You have met this aliasing bug twice already. The mutation and aliasing topic showed one list reached through two names. The signatures and defaults topic showed one default argument reused across calls. Here the same bug hides in a class body.

Not every class attribute is wrong. A value that belongs to the class rather than to any one instance belongs in the class body. A unit string is the usual case, so the fixed Station keeps one.

Your task

The answer box already holds LeakyStation. Leave it broken. Write the rest.

  • leak_demo() builds a LeakyStation named north and one named south. Add the readings 10 and 12 to north only. Return f"south sees {..} readings and LeakyStation.count is {..}". The first slot holds how many readings south can see. The second holds LeakyStation.count.
  • Station with a class attribute UNIT set to "degC" and an __init__ that takes name.
  • add_reading(value) adds one reading to this station.
  • count() returns how many readings this station holds.
  • average() returns the mean of this station's readings rounded to one decimal place. An empty station averages 0.0.
  • label() returns the name and the unit, for example north (degC).

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Create every mutable attribute inside __init__. The fix is one line, so do not rename anything to dodge it.
  • Do not write __slots__, a metaclass, or the copy module. None of them is the answer.
  • Write self as the first parameter of every method.
  • Do not write a method whose name starts with get_ or set_.
  • Do not edit LeakyStation. It is the exhibit, not the exercise.
  • Keep UNIT in the class body. It is the one name that belongs there.
  • Annotate every signature you write. Parameters and the return, and a method that hands back nothing still gets -> None.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

expected.text: south sees 2 readings and LeakyStation.count is 0

testcode.text: north = Station("north") south = Station("south") north.add_reading(10) north.add_reading(13) south.add_reading(4) print(north.count(), south.count()) print(north.average(), south.average()) print(north.label()) print(Station("empty").average())

import inspect src = inspect.getsource(Station) body = src.split("def __init__")[0] assert "[]" not in body, "rule broken: no mutable attribute in the class body" assert "self.readings" in src, "rule broken: readings must be born in __init__" assert "__slots__" not in src, "rule broken: no __slots__" assert "get_" not in src and "set_" not in src, "rule broken: no accessors" assert "copy" not in src, "rule broken: no copy module" a = Station("a") b = Station("b") a.add_reading(1) print(a.readings is b.readings, Station.UNIT, a.UNIT is Station.UNIT)

questiontext.text:
Goal

Rewrite a temperature class so a property replaces its getter and setter pair without one call site changing.

How this works in Python

Java teaches you never to expose a field. Turn celsius from a field into a computed value later and every call site breaks. So you write the pair up front, before anything needs it.

public double getCelsius() {
    return celsius;
}

public void setCelsius(double value) {
    if (value < -273.15) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException(value + " is below absolute zero");
    }
    this.celsius = value;
}

Python removes the reason for the pair. A plain attribute can grow validation later without one call site changing. So you start with the attribute and add the checks only when you need them. The tool that does it is the property.

class Temperature:
    def __init__(self, celsius: float) -> None:
        self.celsius = celsius

    @property
    def celsius(self) -> float:
        return self._celsius

    @celsius.setter
    def celsius(self, value: float) -> None:
        if value < -273.15:
            raise ValueError(f"{value} is below absolute zero")
        self._celsius = value

A line starting with @ above a def is a decorator. It names a function that takes the function below it and hands back a replacement. You write your own decorator later in the course. Here you only apply the ones Python ships.

@property turns celsius into a method that runs on plain attribute access. @celsius.setter attaches the matching method that runs on plain attribute assignment. The call sites never change.

reading = Temperature(21.5)
print(reading.celsius)      # runs the getter
reading.celsius = 40        # runs the setter, which validates
reading.celsius = -300      # raises ValueError

The stored number needs a name of its own. The property already owns the name celsius, so an assignment to self.celsius inside the setter would call the setter again and never stop. The convention is one leading underscore, self._celsius.

Define a getter with no setter and the attribute becomes read only. Assign to it and Python raises AttributeError. That is how you expose a value computed from other values.

Raise, never assert

Reject a bad value with raise ValueError(...). Python has an assert statement, and it looks like the shorter way to write the same check. Run Python with the -O flag and every assert disappears from the program. Your validation disappears with it.

Java's static factory becomes a classmethod.

@classmethod
def from_fahrenheit(cls, value: float) -> "Temperature":
    return cls((value - 32) * 5 / 9)

A classmethod takes the class as its first parameter instead of the instance, and the parameter is named cls by convention. The whole gain comes from writing cls rather than a hard-coded class name. Call BuoyTemperature.from_fahrenheit(32) and cls is BuoyTemperature, so a subclass gets a subclass back. A Java static factory that says new Temperature(...) can never do that. The return type sits in quotes because the class is still being read when Python reaches that line, so the bare name would not resolve.

A staticmethod takes neither self nor cls. It is a plain function that lives in the class namespace because that is where a reader will look for it.

Last, name mangling. Two leading underscores inside a class body are not private.

self.__site = "rig-7"

Python rewrites that name to self._Temperature__site, using the class name. The rewrite stops a subclass from clashing with a name it did not know existed. Anyone who knows the rule can still read the attribute from outside, and the last function below makes you do exactly that.

Your task

The answer box holds the old accessor version and the call sites that use it. Rewrite the class so those call sites work untouched. Write these.

  • Temperature with a class attribute ABSOLUTE_ZERO set to -273.15.
  • __init__(celsius) sets self.__site to "rig-7", then assigns celsius through the property so the validation runs during construction too.
  • A celsius property with a @celsius.setter. A value below ABSOLUTE_ZERO raises ValueError(f"{value} is below absolute zero").
  • A read-only fahrenheit property returning celsius * 9 / 5 + 32.
  • from_fahrenheit(value) as a classmethod built with cls.
  • is_freezing(celsius) as a staticmethod returning whether the value is 0 or below.
  • BuoyTemperature, a subclass of Temperature with an empty body. Python needs a statement there, so write pass, which does nothing on purpose.
  • peek_mangled(reading) reads the mangled attribute from outside the class and returns f"_Temperature__site = {..}" with its value.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Do not leave a method whose name starts with get_ or set_. A hidden test reads your source.
  • Do not add a pair of brackets to a call site. If you edited t.celsius, you solved a different problem.
  • Reject a bad value with raise ValueError. Do not write the word assert.
  • Do not store fahrenheit in __init__. Assigning to it must raise.
  • Build the alternative constructor with cls, never with the name Temperature.
  • Read the mangled attribute by its real name. Do not use getattr tricks or __dict__.
  • Annotate every signature, properties and classmethods included. A getter that hides its return type is a getter you have to read twice.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.
